proxy_language: Hurrian (Hurro-Urartian) as a late, low-confidence regional proxy, supplemented by Proto-Hurro-Urartian reconstructions
proxy_rationale: Hallan Cemi (c. 10th-9th mill. BCE) and Kortik Tepe (c. 10th mill. BCE) are pre-literate Epipalaeolithic/Protoneolithic sites; their language(s) are unknowable and there is no demonstrable continuity to any attested language. The only well-documented language family indigenous to the Upper Tigris/Taurus/Armenian Highland zone in the earliest records is Hurro-Urartian (Hurrian from c. 2300 BCE; Urartian from c. 850 BCE), plausibly a substrate-like survival of an older highland language group. Using it is a defensible regional placeholder, not a claim of descent. Alternatives (Proto-Semitic, Proto-Indo-European, Proto-Kartvelian, Proto-Northeast-Caucasian) are equally unprovable, and Hurrian at least gives phonotactics rooted in the exact geography.
phonology: Hurrian consonants (cuneiform-based interpretation): stops with a voiced/voiceless contrast written b/p, d/t, g/k (probably allophonic or lenis/fortis, with voiced allophones intervocalically); fricatives f (or v), s, sh (written š), z (probably affricate ts), h, kh (written ḫ); nasals m, n; liquids l, r; glides y, w. Vowels: a, e, i, u, with o debated and mostly absent. Vowel length is weakly attested. No reliable tone or stress information. Urartian is similar (adds a possible q/k' series in some analyses).
phonotactics: Syllable shapes (C)V(C); words begin with a single consonant or a vowel (initial vowels are rare); no initial clusters; medial clusters of two consonants are common (e.g. -rt-, -nd-, -ld-, -sh-t-); final clusters are avoided and words typically end in a vowel or in -s, -sh, -m, -n, -l, -r, -d, -t. Voiced stops are not found word-initially in many Hurrian roots (plausible, not certain). Suffix-heavy agglutination means words are often 3-5 syllables when inflected, while bare roots are CV(C) or CVCV.
orthography: Standard Hurrianist transliteration of the cuneiform syllabary in Latin script: b, d, g, p, t, k, f, s, š, z, h, ḫ, m, n, l, r, y, w with vowels a, e, i, u. For game purposes the diacritic-free spellings sh and kh may replace š and ḫ, and the diaeresis/macron forms are avoided. Lowercase, hyphen-separated morphemes in the scholarly style, with compounds and suffixed forms written as one word or hyphenated.
morphology: Agglutinative, ergative-absolutive, suffixing; verbs take long suffix chains. Nouns are formed from roots plus derivational suffixes. Case endings in Hurrian: absolutive -Ø, ergative -sh, genitive -ve/-we/-fe (-ve after vowels, -we/-fe variants), dative -a, directive -ta/-da, comitative -ra, ablative-instrumental -dan/-ten, essive -a, equative -ni(?). Plural -ash (animate)/-na (articulus). The definite article (relator) is -ni (sg.) / -na (pl.). Common nominal derivation: -ni (nominal formative; many nouns end in -ni), -ri/-li/-nni formations, abstract -ushe/-ush. Agent/occupation nouns with -ri/-uri or -ve. Numerals and demonstratives precede or follow depending on form. Vowel-final stems are the norm.
compounding: True compounding is rare in Hurrian; relationships are expressed syntactically with the genitive suffix on the possessor and the possessed head following it (possessor-genitive + head, e.g. X-we Y 'Y of X'). Noun-noun juxtaposition and nominal derivation by suffix (-ri 'one who ...', -ve 'belonging to ...') is the productive way to form place/tool/profession names. For game naming: 'X of Y' = Y-ve X; 'Y-maker/keeper' = Y + agentive suffix; locative via directive/essive -a/-ta.
noun_phrase_order: Modifier/possessor before head: genitive phrase = possessor-ve + head; adjectives usually precede or are suffixed (attributive adjective + noun with agreement via article -ni/-na on the head or, in Urartian, juxtaposition). Demonstratives and numerals precede the noun. Relational/relator suffix attaches to the last word of the noun phrase.
sources: Wegner, Ilse: Einfuhrung in die hurritische Sprache (2nd ed., 2007)
Wilhelm, Gernot: Hurrian, in The Ancient Languages of Syria-Palestine and Arabia (ed. R. Woodard, 2008)
Diakonoff, I.M. and Starostin, S.A.: Hurro-Urartian as an Eastern Caucasian Language (1986)
Starostin database: Hurro-Urartian and Northeast Caucasian etymologies (Tower of Babel project)
Hallan Cemi and Kortik Tepe site reports (Rosenberg; Benz, Coskun, Ozkaya et al.) for archaeological context only
notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic; this language is not Goidelic. These names are Hurrian-inspired placeholders for a culture whose actual language is unrecoverable; treat as speculative. Several glosses above marked with ? are uncertain; builders should prefer the divine names, the case suffixes (-ve genitive, -ni article, -ash plural, -a dative/essive) and the productive suffix patterns over the less-certain root glosses. Keep names vowel-final or ending in sh/n/m/l/r, avoid initial voiced stops, and use the genitive-before-head order.
unit: Upper Tigris Epipalaeolithic-Protoneolithic (Hallan Cemi, Kortik Tepe)
